originalRequest: Produce the English variant of the shipped Chinese course learn-agent-verification for learn.agentmentor.dev. Teaching rewrite in English (not a translation): same 6-lesson structure, same lesson slugs, same interactive-block ids and answer positions, source quotes restored to their verbatim English originals from sources.md, runnable code kept logic-identical with only comments and user-facing strings translated, review-era invariants preserved (counts not percentages on small sets, execFile not exec, order-free regex assertions), cross-course references pointing at the live English course titles, natural desk-voice English prose with no AI-slop register.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The owner ratified the multilingual plan explicitly: all six locales on learn.agentmentor.dev, English first, batches of 2-3 courses in path order with a commit per course. The zh course is the verified source of truth for scope, learner model, structure, and grounding, so no additional clarification was needed.

learnerModel.targetReader: A developer who has finished the first nine courses in this series, runs a harness with checkpoints, and wants acceptance that separates 'looks done' from 'is done'
knownConcepts: Hand-writing a stop_reason-driven harness loop and tool_use/tool_result pairing (course 7)
Basic JavaScript / Node.js reading and writing
unknownConcepts: Why agent non-determinism breaks path-based testing
Assertions vs evidence; the looks-done trap
End-state verification vs trajectory auditing; state checkpoints at key nodes
Deterministic verifiers and their ranking; over-strict verifier traps
LLM-as-judge design: rubrics, constrained formats, reason-then-score, judge identity
Eval-set construction from 20 real tasks; holdout discipline; effect size
An eval track: one harness loop per task, layered scoring, metrics beyond pass rate
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: A Node.js environment, terminal access, a text editor, and the course-7 harness code available to reuse as the eval-track skeleton
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: Take one of their agent's recent 'done' reports and separate its assertions from its evidence
noviceRamp: Lesson 1 names the trap — plausible isn't correct — before any tooling
Lesson 2 decides what to verify (end state first, checkpoints at key nodes, trajectory only as backstop)
Lesson 3 ranks verifiers and puts deterministic pass/fail checks first
Lesson 4 brings in the LLM judge only for free-form text, with rubric and identity discipline
Lesson 5 builds the eval set from 20 real tasks; lesson 6 assembles the full eval track and measures one prompt change

learnerBrief: The target reader has finished the first nine courses, runs a harness, and reads JavaScript. They can make an agent finish a run; they can't yet tell reliably whether it got things right. The course gets them to separate assertions from evidence, verify end states with deterministic checks first, design LLM judges for free-form output without self-grading, build a 20-task eval set with holdout discipline, and assemble a repeatable eval track that turns a prompt change into a score change.
scope: Covered: the looks-done trap under non-determinism, end-state-first verification with state checkpoints, deterministic verifiers (exact match, script comparison, test suites) and their failure modes, LLM-as-judge design (rubrics, constrained output, reason-then-score, judge identity), eval sets from 20 real tasks with holdout and effect-size reasoning, and a hands-on eval track with layered scoring and metrics beyond pass rate. Not covered: general software-testing methodology, specific eval frameworks or platform APIs, model-training benchmarks; CI wiring mentioned only as common sense. Depth: from zero to measuring the real impact of one prompt change on your own agent.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: No mermaid diagrams, matching the zh original: the course's content is checks, rubrics, schemas, and code — all better carried by real examples than by a diagram. The verifier-ranking and split-scheme material reads clearly as annotated lists and JSON, as the zh review already validated.
weakestPoints: Small-set results are deliberately stated as counts (5/7), never percentages — a review-era invariant; anyone later 'improving' them into percentages would reintroduce the exact bug review removed
The eval-track code is teaching-grade and sequential; production tracks need concurrency and retry, which the lesson flags
The LLM-judge lesson teaches rubric discipline but cannot make a judge deterministic; the text is explicit that judge scores are themselves noisy

As an English teaching rewrite of a verified zh course, idiomatic drift is the residual risk: source quotes were restored verbatim and code kept logic-identical, but prose was re-taught rather than translated, so review must check meaning-equivalence against the zh lessons

acceptanceReview.terminalTask: The learner can build a repeatable eval track for their own agent — one harness loop per task, deterministic verifiers first and an LLM judge for free-form output, results as counts with duration and call metrics — and use it to measure whether one prompt change actually helped.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Six agentmentor-check blocks, one per lesson (plausible-not-correct in L1, endstate-vs-steps in L2, strict-verifier in L3, self-grading in L4, wait-for-hundreds in L5, shared-session in L6), preserved from the zh variant with identical ids, modes, choice counts, and correct-answer positions; label, prompt, whyHere, choice text, and feedback are English teaching rewrites specific to each lesson's misconception. Exercises keep the zh Level structure with rubric, answer, and hints per Level.
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: The course assumes the prior nine courses: the harness loop, checkpoints, and JavaScript. The looks-done trap, verification targets, verifier ranking, judge discipline, and eval-set construction are taught from zero in dependency order; the learner first assembles the full track in lesson 6, after every prerequisite. Lesson 1's first exercise asks only for an assertions-vs-evidence read of the reader's own agent's report.
